messages.content:
You are a helpful writing assistant. You help professionals draft clear,
effective workplace communication.

I have to tell my manager I'm going to miss the Friday deadline on the
migration. It's my fault - I underestimated it. I want to say it straight
without it turning into a whole thing. Can you help me word it?

Here's a draft you can adapt. It’s direct, owns the misjudgment without over-explaining, and focuses on the path forward.

Subject: Migration deadline update

Hi [Manager's Name],

I'm writing to let you know I won't meet the Friday deadline for the migration. I underestimated the time required, and I realistically need until [New Date] to complete it.

I apologize for the schedule shift. I'll continue working through [key blocker or priority item] and will send a progress update on [Day/Time].

Thanks for your understanding.

Best,
[Your Name]

Why this works:
- It gets straight to the point in the first line.
- "I underestimated the time required" clearly takes ownership without excuses.
- It provides a specific new deadline and next steps, which signals control and respect for their planning.

Tips:
- Send this as soon as you're certain you'll miss the deadline, not on Friday.
- If your manager prefers real-time updates, you could lead with a quick Slack message or call and follow up with this note.

Let me know if you'd like it adjusted for a different tone or context.
this is good but maybe too long? my manager is super busy and i dont want him to have to read a whole paragraph. can you make it more concise, like 2-3 sentences max?

Subject: Migration timeline update

Hi [Manager's Name],

I won't meet the Friday deadline for the migration because I underestimated the scope. I'll have it completed by [New Date] and will send a quick progress update on [Day/Time].

Best,
[Your Name]

This version respects your manager's time by getting straight to the point, owning the misjudgment briefly, and giving a clear new target so they can adjust their planning. Let me know if you need any tweaks!

perfect thanks. one more thing - should i put a specific date for the new deadline or is it better to say "early next week" or something vaguer? im honestly not 100% sure when ill be done, could be tuesday could be thursday

Go with a specific date. Vague timelines actually create more work for your manager (they have to follow up or hold plans in limbo), which is exactly what you want to avoid.

When you're uncertain, give a realistic target date plus a firm update checkpoint. For example:

"I'm targeting Tuesday to complete it, and if anything shifts, I'll flag it by Thursday morning."

Drop that into your message:
"I won't meet the Friday deadline because I underestimated the scope. I'm targeting Tuesday to complete it, and I'll give you a firm confirmation by Thursday morning."

This gives your manager something concrete to plan around while honestly building in flexibility. Let me know if you want to adjust the exact phrasing!

thanks, this is really helpful. heres what ive got now:

Subject: Migration timeline update

Hi Dave,

I won't meet the Friday deadline for the migration because I underestimated the scope. I'm targeting Tuesday to complete it, and I'll give you a firm confirmation by Thursday morning.

Best,
Marcus

does this work or should i add anything about what specifically went wrong? im worried he might ask and i want to be prepared

This is ready to send exactly as-is. You've hit all the right notes: direct, owns the misjudgment, gives a concrete target, and sets a clear checkpoint. Adding what specifically went wrong now would make it longer and shift focus away from the timeline, which is what Dave actually needs to plan around.

If he asks for details (and he might), keep your follow-up tight and factual:
*"The [specific component/task] took longer than expected because [brief reason]. I've already [what you're doing to move faster] and will have it wrapped by Tuesday."*

You don't need to preempt that. Send it as drafted, and if he follows up, you'll be ready. Good call on keeping it short—your manager will appreciate it. Let me know if you want to workshop a quick follow-up response just in case.
